<reason>Side B won by neutralizing Side A's ecological arguments through green burial mandates and decisively winning the central clash over religious pluralism and class equity. Side A was forced to concede in Rebuttal 2 that composting and alkaline hydrolysis violate non-negotiable religious mandates for observant Muslim and Orthodox Jewish families, falling back on the claim that finite urban land makes eventual exclusion inevitable anyway. Side B dismantled this defense by showing that multi-layered green plots, voluntary alternatives, and transit-connected regional cemeteries extend affordable access for generations, whereas Side A's ban inflicts immediate exclusion on low-income minorities today to prevent a theoretical capacity shortage decades from now.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>Side B's counter in Rebuttal 2 and Closing ([B4.3]-[B4.4], [B5.1]-[B5.3]) seizing on Side A's concession that intact burial is a non-negotiable religious mandate [A4.3] and turning Side A's attack on regional cemeteries as a "deferred eviction" [A5.1] into the devastating point that abolishing public plots today is an "immediate eviction" of working-class religious minorities.</best_rebuttal>
